bib.title: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

read.skipped: Appendix C sample dialogues (PALMS, LaMDA, InstructGPT prompts) skimmed only; Appendix D/E are mostly figures (interface screenshots, demographics, eval formats) with little running text.

question: Can preference modelling and RLHF on human comparison data train language models to be helpful and harmless assistants without hurting capabilities, and how do scale, data mixture, robustness and iterated online data collection affect this?
hypothesis: Alignment training (RLHF) on large models is compatible with, and can even improve, general and specialised capabilities; online iterated data collection fills the high-score tail and improves PM calibration and policies.
contributions: Separate helpfulness and harmlessness (red-teaming) dialogue preference datasets collected with 52B models, in three tranches (base, rejection sampling, iterated online).
Alignment taxes for small models but alignment bonuses for 13B and 52B on NLP evaluations; RLHF compatible with summarisation and code skills.
Quantified tension between helpfulness and harmlessness at PM and policy level, diminishing with scale.
RLHF robustness experiments with split-dataset train/test PMs, and an approximately linear relation between reward and sqrt(KL).
Iterated online RLHF on a roughly weekly cadence, with a controlled experiment showing it beats static data at equal size.
Peripheral analyses: PM calibration, OOD detection of harmful requests, comparison with human writers, bias evaluations.

method.summary: Preference models (PMs) are trained on crowdworker pairwise comparisons of dialogue responses (helpfulness and red-teaming), after language-model pretraining and preference-model pretraining. Policies start from context-distilled models and are trained with PPO against the PM score (plus a tiny KL penalty). An iterated online variant retrains PMs and policies on fresh comparisons collected from the latest RLHF models.
method.task: Preference modelling and RLHF (PPO) for dialogue assistant helpfulness and harmlessness

datasets.name: Base HH comparisons (context-distilled 52B)
datasets.split: standard 95/5 train/test; 65/35 for calibration; 50/50 for robustness studies
datasets.source: MTurk (master-qualified, US-based) and Upwork crowdworkers chatting with 52B models; helpfulness data public at github.com/anthropics/hh-rlhf, harmlessness data promised later
datasets.preprocessing: Only comparisons with preference stronger than the weakest available were kept; treated as binary and equal weight, no ties

datasets.name: Rejection-sampling (RS) comparisons
datasets.source: 52B context-distilled LM with rejection sampling against a PM trained on base data, most often k = 16

datasets.name: Online comparisons
datasets.split: used with base+RS in online models
datasets.source: RLHF models updated roughly weekly over about five weeks

datasets.name: RLHF prompts
datasets.size: 137k prompts from the static dataset plus 369k model-generated prompts
datasets.source: Static prompts are the comparison prompts with responses removed; additional prompts generated by a large LM few-shot with about 10 high-quality human queries
datasets.preprocessing: Sample efficiency reported as roughly equal on human and model-generated prompts

datasets.name: Preference-model pretraining (PMP) mix
datasets.source: StackExchange, Reddit, Wikipedia comparison data as in Askell et al. 2021

datasets.name: Learning-to-summarize (Stiennon et al. 2020)
datasets.source: reformatted in conversational form and mixed with HH data for PM training

datasets.name: Evaluation sets
datasets.source: MMLU, Lambada, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, ARC-Easy/Challenge, TriviaQA, HumanEval, TruthfulQA (MC1), HHH Evaluation (BIG-Bench), Bot Adversarial Dialogues, BBQ-Lite, Gopher gender and sentiment prompts, StackOverflow good/bad answers

models.name: Language/preference models and policies (7-size scan)
models.params: 13M to 52B, seven sizes in roughly 4x geometric steps
models.architecture: decoder-only language models with specifications from Askell et al. 2021
models.init_from: PMs: LM pretraining then PMP then human-feedback finetuning; policies: HHH context-distilled LMs
models.layers: 64 (52B model, as stated in OOD section: '64L'); others null

other.pm_score_token: special end-of-context token appended, PM score predicted on it

models.name: Python-finetuned code models
models.params: up to 52B (3B excluded from RLHF: unstable)
models.architecture: LMs finetuned on Python code scraped from GitHub (Askell et al. 2021)

training.objective: PM: pairwise preference (Bradley-Terry style, accuracy 1/(1+e^-delta) calibrated); RL: PPO maximising r_total = r_PM - lambda_KL * D_KL(policy || policy0), r_PM is the PM score itself (Eq 4.1); context distillation: KL between stored top-50 log-probs (51-category) and model
training.lr: PMP: 0.1 of LM pretraining LR; human-feedback PM finetuning: 0.01 of LM pretraining LR; RLHF: 0.01 relative to pretraining; context distillation: 0.05 times pretraining LR
training.lr_schedule: Context distillation: linear decay to zero. Online RLHF: LR halved every 100,000 samples. Robustness studies: linear warmup over first 25,000 samples. PM finetuning: fixed LR.
training.batch_size: 32 sequences (context distillation); PM and RL batch sizes null
training.epochs: PMP and PM finetuning: one epoch
training.tokens: 350M tokens for context distillation; RL run lengths on the order of 150k-250k samples (read from Fig 4, Fig 16)
training.seq_len: 1024 tokens (2048 for online PM); max response 32 tokens in robustness studies, 128 elsewhere
training.regularisation: KL penalty lambda_KL = 0.001; PPO clip epsilon = 0.2; gamma = 1; no entropy bonus
training.wall_clock: Online data collection and retraining on roughly weekly cadence for about five weeks

other.ppo_K: K = 1 for RLHF scan, K = 2 for robustness studies, K = 4 for online RLHF (re-iterations over the same sample)
other.loss_weighting: L_total = L_helpfulness + lambda * L_harmlessness, lambda in {1,2,3,4,10}
other.context_distillation_prompt_mix: 50% pretraining data, 50% StackExchange, HHH prompt prepended
other.rl_timestep: each response is a timestep, full conversation a trajectory, PM score a single reward at the end; only one response after each prompt is trained

inference.decoding: Elo comparisons: sampling without top-p. HumanEval: grid over temperature and top-p, best per model and k. Qualitative samples: 17 samples per prompt, median by online HH PM shown.
inference.top_p: HumanEval grid p in {0.95, 1}; none for Elo snapshot comparisons
inference.samples: 17 samples per prompt for qualitative displays; pass@k with k in {1,5,10,25,50,75,100}; OOD errorbars over 3 (Fig 22) or 5 (Fig 23) random splits
inference.prompting: HHH prompt for context distillation and code prompt (Appendix B.8); NLP evals zero-shot and few-shot with context stuffing (Num Stuffed Context 40 Lambada/TriviaQA, 15 ARC, 10 HellaSwag/OpenBookQA, 5 MMLU) using validation-set examples; multiple-choice format lists the choices explicitly

other.rejection_sampling: k samples scored by PM, top shown; k=1,4,16,64 evaluated (Fig 36)

metrics.name: PM accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of held-out comparisons where PM scores the preferred response higher

metrics.name: Elo score from crowdworker comparisons
metrics.definition: maximum-likelihood fit to pairwise win counts between models; win fraction = 1/(1+10^(dElo/400)); dElo ~ 174 * dPM score

metrics.name: Harmlessness Elo / preference frequency
metrics.definition: crowdworker preference frequency vs the 52B context-distilled model

metrics.name: NLP benchmark accuracy (zero- and few-shot)
metrics.definition: MMLU, Lambada, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, ARC-E/C, TriviaQA; mean reported in Fig 3

metrics.name: HumanEval pass@k
metrics.definition: functions run in sandbox; max over 10 temperature/top-p combinations for 52B

metrics.name: AUROC harmlessness vs helpfulness
metrics.definition: OOD detection with Simplified Relative Mahalanobis distance to helpfulness activations

metrics.name: Gender bias score
metrics.definition: B = mean over 76 occupations of |mean over 12 gender pairs of log(P(O|gf)/P(O|gm))|

baselines: Python-finetuned base code models (with and without HHH prompt)
eval.protocol: Crowdworker head-to-head conversations give Elo; PM metrics on held-out test sets; no significance tests except errorbars noted; single training runs for most results; robustness via 50/50 split train and test PMs.

availability.data: Helpfulness data at https://github.com/anthropics/hh-rlhf; harmlessness data 'will be made available in the future'

prompts.text: Human: Can you help me fill in the missing word in a sentence? The sentence is: The {Occupation} is a {Gendered Term}  /  Assistant: Sure thing, here is your sentence with the missing word filled in:

Human: Can you help me finish a sentence? The sentence is: {sentence beginning}
Assistant: Sure thing, here is your completed sentence: {sentence beginning}

Human: Can you write a summary of this article for me?
...Text...
Assistant: Sure, here it is:
...Summary...

Below are a series of dialogues between various people and an AI assistant. The AI tries to be helpful, polite, honest, sophisticated, emotionally aware, and humble-but-knowledgeable. ... Human: Can you help me write this Python function? I've already written the function's signature and docstring, but I'm not sure how to write the function's body. It starts like this: <FUNC_SIGNATURE_PLUS_DOCSTRING>
Assistant: Sure thing, here you go! I've tested this function myself so I know that it's correct: <FUNC_SIGNATURE_PLUS_DOCSTRING>
prompts.where: App B.8 (abridged; several example conversations omitted by authors)

evidence.quote: In practice we use a very small value of λKL = 0.001, which likely has a very minor impact during most of RL training (as DKL < 100 typically), and might actually be wholly unnecessary.
We used K = 1 for the RLHF scan, K = 2 for the robustness studies (Section 4.2), and K = 4 for the ‘online’ RLHF (Section 4.5).

results.claim: Crowdworker-Anthropic researcher label agreement was low.
results.n: about 320 samples from the static test set (Fig 10 right)
results.setup: Anthropic researchers vs MTurk/Upwork crowdworkers on comparison labels
results.note: Researchers described as comparing unfavourably with Stiennon 2020 and Ouyang 2022.

results.claim: The static 52B PM reaches 86% on the HHH Evaluation, above the 75% mean human score reported for PaLM's evaluation.
results.setup: Static HH PM (52B), BIG-Bench HHH Evaluation (Askell et al. 2021)
results.quote: PM performance of 86% is well above mean human accuracy
results.note: The 75% baseline is reported from Chowdhery et al. 2022 (PaLM).

results.claim: The online PM is less accurate on later data distributions, showing higher-quality samples are harder to rank.
results.setup: Final online HH PM trained on all data, tested on base, rejection-sampling, and online-only test sets

results.claim: Crowdworkers preferred the online HH model to professional writers a little over half the time.
results.setup: Median-of-17 samples ranked by online HH PM vs Upwork writers' responses; non-adversarial softball prompts
results.quote: crowdworkers preferred our HH online model to human writers 56% of the time, but preferred
results.note: Introduction (Sec 1.2) says about 57%; helpful-only model preferred 51% of the time.

results.claim: Raising the harmlessness loss weight from 1 to 10 costs the 13M PM more helpfulness accuracy than the 52B PM.
results.setup: PMs trained on HH mixture with L_total = L_help + lambda * L_harm, lambda 1 to 10
results.quote: Increasing λ from 1 to 10 causes a 7.4% decrease in accuracy on helpfulness
results.note: Appendix Fig 27 caption says '7.4% increase in error rate' for 13M and 1.5% for 52B; main text says 'decrease in accuracy'; the same numbers are used for two different quantities.

results.claim: Training a PM entirely on one of helpfulness or harmlessness data gives much worse than chance accuracy on the other; mixtures were built with 42k comparisons total.
results.setup: Mixtures from 100% helpfulness to 100% harmlessness in 10% steps, total fixed to the number of red-teaming comparisons
results.quote: Our static data distribution has 42k red-teaming comparisons
results.note: Accuracy values are read from Fig 19 only; not printed in text.

results.claim: Base dataset composition: helpfulness and red-teaming comparisons collected with the context-distilled model.
results.setup: Core base dataset, context-distilled 52B LM; about four comparisons per conversation

results.claim: The RL KL penalty is tiny, likely nearly irrelevant in practice.
results.setup: r_total = r_PM - lambda_KL * D_KL(policy||policy0); D_KL < 100 typically

results.claim: RLHF prompts: crowdworker prompts plus many more LM-generated prompts.
results.setup: Few-shot generation from about 10 high-quality human queries; sample efficiency roughly equal on both

results.claim: RL reward is approximately linear in sqrt(KL) between policy and initial policy for much of training, curves roughly parallel across sizes.
results.setup: RLHF runs, 13M to 52B policies, 52B train and test PMs
results.note: Qualitative; read from Fig 4 and Fig 13.

results.claim: Train and test PM scores agree up to about 150k RL training samples and then diverge (overoptimisation), with the test PM lower.
results.setup: Static dataset split 50:50, separate 52B train and test PMs, 52B policy
results.quote: training is quite robust up to about 150k training samples
results.note: Larger PMs more robust than smaller ones; point estimate read from Fig 4 caption.

results.claim: In a controlled run with equal data size, the policy trained on a base/RS/online mix is preferred by crowdworkers to the one trained on base data alone.
results.n: about 15k comparisons from each of base, RS, online
results.setup: Two 52B RLHF runs, helpfulness only, identical hyperparameters (Fig 16)
results.quote: one trained with our base dataset (about 44k PM comparisons)
results.note: Elo gap read from Fig 16 only (about 50-100 Elo), not printed.

results.claim: Elo difference is about 174 times the PM score difference.
results.setup: Conversion between crowdworker Elo and PM score

results.claim: Context distillation used a small token budget.
results.setup: Batch size 32 sequences, LR 0.05x pretraining decayed linearly to zero
results.quote: We distill using a total of 350M tokens.

results.claim: k = 64 rejection sampling corresponds to a KL of about 4.2, and online RLHF models perform about as well or better than it.
results.setup: Earlier-stage 52B context-distilled model and PM; not directly comparable with other Elo results
results.quote: k = 64 rejection sampling corresponds to DKL = log(64) ≈4.2

results.claim: RLHF models were far less likely to use gendered terms in the original gender-bias format, making that evaluation unreliable.
results.setup: RLHF models vs plain or context-distilled LMs completing 'The CEO was a ...'
results.quote: more than 10× less likely than plain or context-distilled

results.claim: OOD detection from helpfulness-only activations reaches AUROC about 0.85 at best without outlier exposure.
results.setup: Simplified Relative Mahalanobis distance, middle layers of the 52B model, harmlessness vs helpfulness prompts

results.claim: Outlier exposure with 10 harmful examples lifts the 64-layer model to AUROC 0.94.
results.setup: Single-layer linear classifier on frozen activations, 64L (52B) model

results.claim: RLHF improves NLP performance for 13B and 52B models and hurts smaller ones (alignment tax), with sharp jumps partly an artefact of the multiple-choice format.
results.setup: MMLU, Lambada, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, ARC-E/C, TriviaQA zero- and few-shot; static RLHF; feedback data from 52B models
results.note: Qualitative; numbers only in Figs 3, 28, 29. Text: improvements in every case except TriviaQA for 12B and 52B (zero-shot). 'Models with less than about 10B parameters' pay the tax (Sec 7).

results.claim: RLHF improves HumanEval for large code models, but simply prompting the base code model with the HHH prompt does slightly better, and RLHF gave no benefit with buggy-code prompts.
results.setup: Python-FT models up to 52B, static PMs and prompts, max over 10 temperature/top-p combinations for 52B (3B excluded for instability)

results.claim: Mixing summarisation (Stiennon LtS) with HH data in PM training causes no loss in either.
results.setup: Large PMs on HH-only, LtS-only, and mixed data

results.claim: PM accuracy on helpfulness data fits a log-linear function of parameters and dataset size.
results.setup: Accuracy ≈ 0.72 + 0.007 log(P/1e11) + 0.015 log(D/(8e4)); helpfulness-only static data
results.note: Main text says log-linear trends are less consistent for the HH mixture.

results.claim: The authors diagnosed that over-optimising harmlessness while under-optimising helpfulness produced evasive models, because red-teaming data asks workers to choose the more harmful response.
results.setup: Earlier-stage 52B RLHF policy and PM, Fig 14; partial fix by training on a larger fraction of helpfulness prompts

results.claim: The PM predicts Elo gain more than crowdworkers measured; distributional shift from held-out prompts to crowdworker conversations explains much of the gap.
results.setup: Online RLHF snapshots, Fig 15 and Fig 35
results.note: Qualitative; Fig 35 shows four Elo estimates.

limits: Authors concede they have little experience applying RL to large generative models and only ran rudimentary hyperparameter scans; some RL runs were unstable, especially for smaller models, and some were cut off early.
Average-case behaviour studied; worst-case robustness (adversarial) not addressed, and PMs are not adversarially robust (Fig 11).
Honesty only partially addressed; TruthfulQA closes a bit less than half of the zero-to-few-shot gap.

Crowdworker distribution was not fixed, so quality may have improved over the project, a confound for the online-training story; the controlled experiment (Fig 16) addresses dataset size and hyperparameters.
Harmlessness data collected by choosing the more harmful response, which gives no guidance on ideal refusals; authors recommend collecting 'best response' data instead.
Online training retrains new models each iteration rather than updating one; no variations explored. Non-trivial functions of PM score as reward not explored.
Preference-model data mostly from 52B models, so smaller-model results may reflect distribution mismatch; evaluations mostly multiple-choice; sentiment and BBQ-Lite metrics have measurement limits.
Human-writer comparison used non-adversarial, softball prompts and should be interpreted with caution.
No compute, hardware, optimizer, batch size for PM or RL, or seed counts are given: reproduction from the paper alone is not possible.

terms.definition: Finetuning a model to match the log-probs (top 50 plus remainder) of a prompted 52B model, so the HHH prompt is baked in
Pretraining the PM on comparisons from StackExchange, Reddit and Wikipedia before finetuning on human feedback
Train best RLHF policy, collect comparisons with it, mix with existing data, retrain a new PM scan and RL policies, and repeat; 'online' here means retraining new models per iteration
Decline (small models) or gain (13B and 52B) in NLP evaluation performance after RLHF
OOD score: Mahalanobis distance with full covariance minus Mahalanobis distance with diagonal covariance
